In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the storage capacity and selectivity of CO2/CH4 are not necessarily correlated.
C(168) is the most selective material among these three frameworks.
C(168) has the greatest adsorption capacity for CH(3) and CO(3), and it also has the highest adsorption selectivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
silicalite and C(168), which are microporous and nanoporous, respectively, are promising materials for CO(2)/ CH(4) separation.
C(168) is a better candidate for the separation of CO(2)/ CH(4) mixture.
the adsorption and diffusion of CH(4) are more sensitive to the pore structure and the interaction with the framework than those of CO(2).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the storage and separation selectivity are two different properties and should be evaluated separately.
C(168) is the most selective material for the separation of CO(2)/ CH(4) mixture at the expense of its storage capacity.
C(168) is an attractive material to be explored for CO(2)/ CH(4) separation.
